lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Well, Alexander. At this point you can hardly deny you are my son. You would not be dead if you were Ammon’s.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I was never confused about that myself, father. I knew I was the son of Philip, son of Amyntas. I accepted the oracle because I thought it would be useful for business.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Useful? You thought it useful to put yourself in a position to be conned by temple staff?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Not that. The barbarians were terrified of me. Once they thought they were fighting a god, nobody wanted to stand up to me. It made them easier to beat.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And whom exactly did you beat that was worth beating? You spent your time running into cowards hiding behind little bows, little shields, and wicker screens. Beating Greeks—that would have been something: Boeotians, Phocians, Athenians; Arcadian heavy infantry, Thessalian cavalry, Elean javelin-men, Mantinean peltasts; or Thracians, Illyrians, Paeonians. Those are serious jobs. But Medes and Persians and Chaldaeans—soft people jingling with gold? You do remember, before you, ten thousand men went up with Clearchus and beat them too. They would not even come to grips; they ran before the arrows got there.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: The Scythians, father, and the elephants of India were not exactly negligible. And I beat them without splitting them against each other, without buying victories by treachery. I never broke an oath, never lied under promise, never did anything dishonourable just to win. As for the Greeks, most of them came over without bloodshed. The Thebans—well, you have probably heard how I dealt with them.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I have heard all of it. Cleitus told me—the man you ran through with a spear while he was at dinner, because he dared to praise me against your achievements.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And then you threw off the Macedonian cloak, put on a Persian candys, so they say, stuck the upright tiara on your head, and expected Macedonians—free men—to prostrate themselves to you. Funniest of all, you copied the people you had beaten. I will pass over the rest: shutting educated men in with lions, marrying the way you did, making a religion of Hephaestion. I did approve of one thing when I heard it: you kept away from Darius’ wife, though she was beautiful, and you cared for his mother and daughters. That was kingly.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And my love of danger, father? You do not praise that? Being the first down inside the wall among the Oxydracae, taking all those wounds?

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: No, Alexander, I do not praise that. Not because I think it is not noble for a king to be wounded now and then and risk himself in front of the army, but because in your particular case it was disastrous branding. If a man is supposed to be a god, and then he gets wounded, and everyone sees him carried out of battle on a stretcher, pouring blood and howling over the injury, that is comedy. It exposes Ammon as a fraud and a lying oracle, and the prophets as flatterers. Who would not laugh at the son of Zeus fainting and begging the doctors to help him? And now that you are dead, do you not suppose plenty of people are mocking the whole performance—seeing the corpse of the god lying flat, already rotting and swelling, according to the usual regulations for bodies? Besides, this ‘useful’ thing you mention—winning easily because of the god routine—took a great deal away from the glory of what you achieved. Everything looks smaller when people think a god did it.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: That is not how people think of me. They set me beside Heracles and Dionysus. And Aornus—the rock neither of them took—I alone captured.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: You see? That is exactly how the son of Ammon talks: comparing himself with Heracles and Dionysus. Are you not embarrassed, Alexander? Will you never unlearn the smoke and learn who you are—especially now that you are dead?
